story: A cold, pale world that does things sideways.
hints: That axial tilt means it’s spinning on its side.
Neptune’s year is about 165 Earth years. This one is half that.
why: Tipped over at about 98°, so it rolls around the Sun on its side, with an 84-year orbit and the coldest atmosphere measured on any planet, down to about −224 °C. It’s Uranus. Neptune is the natural guess, but Neptune is further out, takes about 165 years to orbit and isn’t lying down on the job.
pearl: Because of the tilt, each pole gets about 42 years of sunlight followed by about 42 years of darkness.

story: Islands, bullet trains and a lot of birthday cakes with 100 candles.

panels.name: Compared with a typical country
rows: Early classic novel written by a woman (c. 1010)

hints: People here live a very long time.
A court lady wrote a famous novel about a thousand years ago.
Early classic novel written by a woman (c. 1010)
key: Early classic novel written by a woman (c. 1010)
why: About 124 million people across 14,125 islands, life expectancy around 84, and nearly 100,000 people aged 100 or over (nearly 9 in 10 are women). It’s Japan. Indonesia has more islands, but nowhere near as many centenarians. Picking New Zealand was brave. Wrong, but brave.
pearl: The Tale of Genji, by Murasaki Shikibu, a woman at the Japanese imperial court, is often called the world’s first novel.

story: Very tall, very calm and always first to see rain coming.

panels.name: Compared with a typical large mammal

hints: Check the height. It’s not a typo.
Pumping blood up that neck takes serious pressure.
why: Up to about 5.5 m tall, a tongue around 45 cm long, blood pressure about double ours to push blood up to the brain, and a 1.5-metre drop at birth. It’s a giraffe. Fun twist: its neck has 7 bones, the same as yours. Picked the ostrich? Tall, yes. Mammal, no.
pearl: The okapi is the giraffe’s closest living relative. It looks like a zebra-horse mix but has the same long, dark tongue.

story: Where the bus is a boat and the streets are wet.

panels.name: Compared with a typical European city

hints: Count the islands. Then look for the cars.
Lots of visitors, very few locals.
why: About 118 islands joined by roughly 400 bridges, no cars at all in the historic centre, and fewer than 50,000 residents there since 2022. It’s Venice. Amsterdam is a respectable guess. But you can’t cycle up to a gondola.
pearl: In 2010, Giorgia Boscolo became Venice’s first licensed female gondolier, breaking about 900 years of men-only tradition.

story: A famous lady who has held the same pose since 1886.

panels.name: Compared with a typical public statue

hints: She stands on an island and gets hit by lightning a lot.
why: A copper skin only about as thick as two coins (about 2.4 mm), weathered green, 46 m from heel to torch, dedicated in 1886 and reportedly struck by lightning around 600 times a year. It’s the Statue of Liberty. Her inner frame was designed by Gustave Eiffel, yes, that Eiffel. The Little Mermaid is just 1.25 m tall. Close, if you squint.
pearl: The poem on her pedestal, ‘The New Colossus’ (‘Give me your tired, your poor…’), was written by Emma Lazarus in 1883.

story: Lives underground in a colony with a queen. No, not a bee.
hints: This rodent lives about ten times longer than it should.
One queen runs a huge colony. Like an ant nest with teeth.
why: A rodent that can live more than 37 years, survive about 18 minutes without oxygen, barely regulates its own temperature and lives in colonies of around 80 with a single breeding queen. It’s the naked mole-rat. The Damaraland mole-rat also has a queen, so that guess was clever. Just not long-lived enough.
pearl: Naked mole-rats very rarely get cancer, which is why scientists study them closely.

story: Big skies, lots of space and more horses than people.
hints: The emptiest country on Earth, with the coldest capital.
why: The least densely populated country in the world at about 2 people per km², roughly 4.7 million horses for 3.5 million people, nearly 58 million farm animals, and Ulaanbaatar, the coldest capital city, averaging about −21 °C in January. It’s Mongolia. Kazakhstan was a sensible guess. But it has fewer horses per person.
pearl: Nearly half of all Mongolians live in Ulaanbaatar, yet many families still move with their herds and live in a ger (yurt).

story: Has weather, rivers, lakes and rain. Just not the kind you know.
hints: Thicker air than Earth, on something so small and cold?
Lakes and rivers, but not of water.
why: The only moon with a thick atmosphere (mostly nitrogen, like ours, at about 1.5 times Earth’s surface pressure), lakes and rain of liquid methane at about −180 °C, and a day of about 16 Earth days. It’s Titan, Saturn’s largest moon. Ganymede is a sharp guess, as it’s a bit bigger, but it has almost no air.
pearl: Titan is bigger than the planet Mercury. In 2005 the Huygens probe landed there, the furthest landing ever made.

story: Rainforest, football and your morning coffee.

panels.name: Compared with a typical country
rows: Home of the all-time top World Cup scorer

hints: Check the coffee share and the football trophies.
She has scored more World Cup goals than anyone, man or woman.
Home of the all-time top World Cup scorer
key: Home of the all-time top World Cup scorer
why: The world’s biggest coffee grower (about a third of the world’s beans), five men’s World Cups, about 60% of the Amazon, and Marta, who has scored 17 World Cup goals, more than any player in history. It’s Brazil. Argentina is a fair shout on football, but it doesn’t grow much coffee.
pearl: Brazil has been the world’s largest coffee producer for more than 150 years.

story: Sleepy, fussy eater, lives up a tree.

panels.name: Compared with a typical tree-dwelling mammal

hints: Its fingerprints could confuse a detective.
why: Sleeps about 18 to 22 hours a day to cope with a low-energy eucalyptus diet, has two thumbs on each hand and fingerprints almost impossible to tell apart from ours, and is born about the size of a peanut. It’s a koala. Picked the sloth? Good instinct for naps. Wrong continent.
pearl: Koalas are marsupials, not bears. A newborn joey lives in its mother’s pouch for about six months.

story: Neon, trains on time and a lot of very good dinners.

panels.name: Compared with a typical big city

hints: Someone’s eating well. Look at the stars.
One station handles more people a day than most cities have.
why: Around 37 million people in the greater area, more Michelin-starred restaurants than any other city (about 190 in the 2026 guide) and Shinjuku, the world’s busiest station, with about 3.5 million passengers a day. It’s Tokyo. Paris has fewer stars. Don’t tell Paris.
pearl: Shinjuku Station has about 200 exits. Getting lost there is practically a local tradition.

story: Often hidden by fog. Very orange underneath.

panels.name: Compared with a typical big suspension bridge

hints: That colour has its own name.
The longest suspension span in the world from 1937 to 1964.
why: A 1,280 m main span (the world’s longest from 1937 until 1964), towers 227 m above the water, about 129,000 km of wire in each main cable (more than three laps of Earth), all painted International Orange. It’s the Golden Gate Bridge. Tower Bridge is a lovely guess. But it opens up. It doesn’t hang.
pearl: The orange was first chosen as a primer. The architect liked how it stood out in the fog and kept it.

story: Cold water, slow life, very long memory.
hints: Look at how long it lives.
Slow and very cold. Think Arctic.
why: Estimated to live about 400 years (somewhere between 272 and 512), growing about a centimetre a year, not grown up until about 150, cruising at about 1 km/h in near-freezing Arctic water. It’s the Greenland shark, the longest-lived animal with a backbone. The ocean quahog clam can live over 500 years, a clever pick, but it’s a clam.
pearl: Some Greenland sharks swimming today may have hatched in the 1600s, or even earlier.

story: Fire, ice and very warm swimming pools.
hints: Most houses are heated by the ground.
why: Only about 390,000 people, nearly all electricity from hydro and geothermal, about 9 in 10 homes heated by hot water from the ground, more electricity made per person than anywhere, and no McDonald’s since 2009. It’s Iceland. Norway also runs almost all on renewables, so that guess was sharp. But Norway heats with electricity, not volcanoes.
pearl: In 1980 Iceland elected Vigdís Finnbogadóttir, the world’s first woman voted in as president in a national election.

story: Small, fast and either baking or freezing.
hints: Its year is shorter than its day.
Huge swing from day to night, and almost all core.
why: An 88-day year but 176 Earth days from one sunrise to the next, 430 °C by day and −180 °C at night, and an iron core about 85% of its width. It’s Mercury. Mars has exactly the same gravity (0.38), so that guess was a proper trap. But Mars’ day is about 24.6 hours.
pearl: Despite being closest to the Sun, Mercury probably has water ice hiding in permanently shadowed craters at its poles.

story: Huge, chilly in places and very sweet on syrup.
hints: The longest coastline in the world.
Only one neighbour, and a lot of maple trees.
why: The world’s longest coastline at about 243,000 km, the second-largest country, only about 4 people per km², a single land neighbour, and over 75% of the world’s maple syrup. It’s Canada. Russia is bigger, but it borders 14 countries. Chose Norway? Pretty fjords, wrong syrup.
pearl: In 1992 neurologist Roberta Bondar became Canada’s first woman in space, flying on the Space Shuttle Discovery.

story: Huge, smart and run by grandmothers.

panels.name: Compared with a typical large land mammal

hints: Nearly two years to make a baby.
The herd follows its wise old matriarch.
why: About 6 tonnes, a 22-month pregnancy (the longest of any land mammal), only about 2 hours of sleep a night in the wild, and herds led by the oldest female. It’s the African elephant, the largest animal on land. Picked the blue whale? Big thinking. Wet thinking.
pearl: Matriarchs remember water holes and dangers for decades, and herds with older leaders tend to survive droughts better.

story: Breathtaking views. Literally.

panels.name: Compared with a typical capital city

hints: Very high up. Pasta takes longer here.
Commuters ride to work in the sky.
why: About 3,640 m up, where water boils at roughly 88 °C, and home to Mi Teleférico, the world’s largest urban cable car network at about 30 km over 10 lines. It’s La Paz, Bolivia. Lhasa is almost exactly as high, so nice try. But it doesn’t commute by gondola.
pearl: The ‘Cholita climbers’, Indigenous Aymara women, climb some of South America’s highest peaks wearing their traditional layered skirts.

story: A stone city in the clouds that kept a low profile for centuries.

panels.name: Compared with a typical ancient site

hints: High in the mountains. Think Andes.
Stones cut so precisely they need no glue.
why: Perched about 2,430 m up on an Andean ridge, built around 1450, about 200 stone structures fitted without mortar, and brought to world attention in 1911. It’s Machu Picchu, Peru. Teotihuacan is nearly as high, so good thinking, but it’s well over 1,000 years older and sits in a wide valley, not on a ridge.
pearl: The fitted stone walls helped the buildings ride out earthquakes: the stones can shift slightly and settle back into place.

story: Forever young, always smiling, regrows what it loses.

panels.name: Compared with a typical salamander
rows: Keeps its gills as an adult

hints: It only lives wild in one place, near a capital city.
key: Keeps its gills as an adult
why: Keeps its feathery gills for life, regrows limbs, spinal cord and even parts of its heart, has a genome about 10 times bigger than ours (about 32 billion letters), and lives wild only in the canals of Xochimilco in Mexico City. It’s the axolotl. The olm also keeps its gills, so that guess was a thinker, but it lives in dark caves in the Balkans, including Slovenia.
pearl: Axolotls come in pink, gold and dark ‘wild’ colours. Almost all the pink ones are bred in aquariums.

story: Small, green and seriously into beef and football.

panels.name: Compared with a typical country
rows: First men’s World Cup host and winner
First to give every school child a laptop

hints: It hosted and won the very first World Cup in 1930.
First men’s World Cup host and winner
key: First men’s World Cup host and winner
why: About 3.4 million people and roughly 12 million cattle (about 3.5 per person), most electricity from wind, hydro and other renewables, the 1930 World Cup host and champion, and the first country to give every primary student a laptop. It’s Uruguay. Argentina is the obvious neighbour guess, but it has far more people per cow.
pearl: Uruguay’s ‘One Laptop per Child’ program, Plan Ceibal, began in 2007 and reached every public primary school student.

story: The most volcanic place in the solar system.
hints: Those plumes are ten times taller than any Earth eruption.
Bone dry and coated in sulphur.
why: About 400 active volcanoes, plumes reaching around 400 km high, a yellow sulphur-stained surface and almost no water, on a moon just a bit bigger than ours. It’s Io, Jupiter’s innermost large moon. Enceladus has plumes too, so that pick had logic, but they spray ice, not lava.
pearl: Io’s heat comes from Jupiter’s gravity squeezing and stretching it, like a stress ball, as it orbits about every 42 hours.

story: Very dry, very old and lives along one river.

panels.name: Compared with a typical country
rows: Years its tallest building held the world record

hints: Hardly any rain, so everyone lives by the river.
One tomb was the tallest structure on Earth for nearly 4,000 years.
Years its tallest building held the world record
key: Years its tallest building held the world record
why: About 108 million people, roughly 51 mm of rain a year on average, about 97% of the population living in the Nile valley and delta, and a Great Pyramid that was the world’s tallest human-made structure for around 3,800 years. It’s Egypt. Sudan is a crafty guess: it actually has more pyramids than Egypt.
pearl: Hatshepsut ruled Egypt as pharaoh for about 20 years around 1470 BC and is remembered for her trade expeditions and huge building projects.

story: Hangs around all day and takes life very, very slowly.
hints: Check the top speed. That’s a decimal point.
Green fur and one bathroom trip a week.
why: A top speed of about 0.24 km/h, one trip down the tree a week to go to the toilet, a lowish body temperature, algae growing in its fur, and extra neck bones (9 instead of the usual 7) for turning its head. It’s a three-toed sloth. Picked the koala? Great nap energy, wrong rainforest.
pearl: Sloths are surprisingly good swimmers, moving about three times faster in water than on land.

story: Hot, humid, green and growing. Physically.

panels.name: Compared with a typical big city
rows: Street-food stall with a Michelin star

hints: This city keeps making more land.
Street-food stall with a Michelin star
key: Street-food stall with a Michelin star
why: Grown from about 582 km² to about 745 km² by reclaiming land from the sea, around 82% humidity and about 2,340 mm of rain a year, a highest point of just 164 m, and hawker stalls that have won Michelin stars. It’s Singapore. Dubai has reclaimed land too, a reasonable pick, but it gets about 100 mm of rain a year.
pearl: In 2016 a soya sauce chicken stall at Chinatown Complex became one of the world’s first street-food stalls to earn a Michelin star.

story: Very tall. No, taller than that.

panels.name: Compared with a typical supertall skyscraper
rows: Top cooler than the base by

hints: Nothing else is this tall. Nothing.
why: 828 m tall with 163 floors, opened in 2010, visible from about 95 km away, and up to 6 °C cooler at the top than at street level. It’s the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, the tallest building in the world. Merdeka 118 in Kuala Lumpur is second at about 679 m, a smart pick, but nearly 150 m short.
pearl: The Burj Khalifa took about six years to build and is covered in about 26,000 glass panels.

story: Stocky, burrowing and surprisingly quick off the mark.

panels.name: Compared with a typical burrowing mammal

hints: A backwards pouch keeps dirt out while digging.
The poo is the giveaway. Look at the shape.
why: Sprints at up to about 40 km/h, has a backwards-facing pouch so it doesn’t fill with dirt while digging, and leaves around 80 to 100 cube-shaped droppings a night to mark its patch. It’s a wombat. Picked the badger? Good digger, round poo.
pearl: Wombats are the only animals known to make cube-shaped poo, which helps it stay put on rocks and logs.

story: Small, green and buzzing.
hints: Very short coast, lots of caves underneath.
why: About 2.1 million people, nearly 60% forest, almost 16,000 registered caves, about 5 beekeepers per 1,000 people and only about 47 km of coastline. It’s Slovenia. Slovakia is the classic mix-up, and no shame in it. But Slovakia has no coast at all.
pearl: Climber Janja Garnbret, widely called the best sport climber ever, won Olympic gold for Slovenia in 2021 and 2024. Slovenia also proposed World Bee Day (20 May).

story: Icy on the outside, maybe very interesting on the inside.
hints: A moon smaller than ours with more water than Earth.
A very thick ice shell on top.
why: Slightly smaller than our Moon, about −160 °C at the equator, with an ice shell roughly 15 to 25 km thick over a salty ocean that may hold about twice as much water as all of Earth’s oceans. It’s Europa, one of Jupiter’s moons. Enceladus also hides an ocean, so that guess had brains, but it’s tiny, only about 500 km across.
pearl: NASA’s Europa Clipper launched in 2024 and is due to reach Jupiter in 2030 to study whether Europa could support life.

story: Pasta, history and two whole countries tucked inside.

panels.name: Compared with a typical country
rows: First woman to earn a university doctorate

hints: More World Heritage Sites than any other country, and two countries inside it.
why: More UNESCO World Heritage Sites than any other country (62), about 23 kg of pasta per person a year, and San Marino and Vatican City sitting entirely inside its borders. It’s Italy. Picked France? Lovely food, but it eats far less pasta.
pearl: In 1678 Elena Cornaro Piscopia earned a doctorate at the University of Padua, the first woman known to receive a doctoral degree.
